title: Japanese is not English: expression strategies
summary: Japanese does the work of English pronouns with the zero pronoun, その, ある and the favor verbs, so you do not need a word for it, he or she.

blocks.text: Languages differ in their **expression strategies**: what they say with a pronoun, Japanese may say with structure. English cannot get through a paragraph without **it**; Japanese has **no word for it**, only zero. Even I and you are not true pronouns: 私, 僕, 俺 and あなた, お前 are roundabout ways of pointing at yourself and others, and textbook sentences full of 私 and あなた are unnatural. Calling a teacher or boss **あなた** is rude; use their name or title.

**その** is not just "that": it means the related one, the thing in question, so さくらとその犬 is "Sakura and her dog". **ある日** (an existing day) starts stories: "one day". And the favor verbs tell who did what to whom: 教えてくれた contains no he and no me, but くれる says someone else did it for me. A plain future action defaults to I.

blocks.jp: さくらとその犬が公園に来た。
blocks.en: Sakura and her dog came to the park.

blocks.jp: ある日、森で熊に会った。
blocks.en: One day I met a bear in the forest.

blocks.text: 彼 and 彼女 were brought in during the late Edo and Meiji eras to translate European novels. They are used today, but the zero pronoun is far more common.

items: I and you: mostly zero or a name; あなた can be rude.
**その** = related to the topic; **ある日** = one day.
**くれる / あげる / もらう** show who does it for whom.

questions.instruction: How do you start a story with "one day"?
questions.note: ある日 (an existing day) opens a story.

questions.prompt: さくらには犬がいる。＿＿犬の名前はポチだ。
questions.note: その points to the related thing already in the topic: her dog.
questions.en: Sakura has a dog. The dog's name is Pochi.

questions.prompt: Japanese needs a word for "it" in every sentence.
questions.note: Japanese has no word for it: it uses zero.

questions.prompt: 友だちが日本語を教えてくれた。
questions.note: くれる says someone did it for me.

questions.prompt: 弟に本を買ってあげた。
questions.note: あげる: I did it for someone else.
questions.en: I bought my younger brother a book.

questions.prompt: 先生に漢字を教えてもらった。
questions.note: もらう: I received the favor from the person marked に.
questions.en: I had the teacher teach me kanji.

questions.note: A plain action about the future defaults to I.
questions.en: I am going to school tomorrow.

questions.instruction: Which is rude to call your teacher?
questions.note: Use a name or title for a teacher or boss, never あなた.

questions.instruction: Why do 彼 and 彼女 appear in Japanese?
options: They were brought in to translate European novels
They are ancient words from poems
questions.note: Late Edo and Meiji translators needed words for he and she.
あげる shows I do it for you, so no pronoun is needed.

questions.instruction: Tap the word that shows someone did it for me
questions.note: くれた carries the 'for me'.
questions.en: My mother made me a lunch box.

questions.instruction: Tap the word that opens a story
questions.note: ある日 is the storytelling "one day".
questions.en: One day, I met a friend at the station.

questions.instruction: Which is the more natural way to say "I ate breakfast"?
options: 私は私の朝ごはんを食べました
朝ごはんを食べました
あなたは朝ごはんを食べました
彼が朝ごはんを食べました
questions.note: The zero pronoun is far more common than 私は私の...

questions.prompt: Calling your boss あなた is polite.
questions.note: あなた is rude toward a boss or teacher.

questions.instruction: 教えてくれた has no word for "me". What shows it?
questions.note: くれる says someone else did it for me.

questions.prompt: One day I found money on the road.
questions.note: ある日 opens, and the zero pronoun hides I.
questions.en: One day I found money on the road.

questions.prompt: 友だちが私にプレゼントをくれた。
questions.note: くれる: the giver is the one marked が, and the receiver is me.
questions.en: A friend gave me a present.

questions.prompt: 私は妹にプレゼントを買って＿＿。
questions.note: I did it for my sister: あげる.
questions.en: I bought my sister a present.

questions.note: A plain action in the present defaults to I.

questions.prompt: 私 and あなた are true pronouns in Japanese.
questions.note: They are roundabout ways of pointing at yourself and others.
questions.en: 私, あなた: I, you.

questions.prompt: 田中さんとその友だちが来た。
questions.note: その means the related one: Tanaka's.
